Microsoft Fabric

Source: vignettes/fabric.Rmd
fabric.Rmd

Microsoft Fabric stores and queries analytics data in warehouses, lakehouses and other services. You can use that data in a Shiny app with each visitor’s Microsoft account and existing access permissions.

Start with a SQL endpoint: a Warehouse, Lakehouse SQL endpoint or SQL Database can supply a DBI connection for SQL and dbplyr queries. Later in this guide, the same sign-in lets you call fabricQueryR functions to list workspaces or read Lakehouse tables.

Try the guided demo

Run shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("fabric") in the R console for an editable local app. The launcher helps you find the SQL endpoint and Microsoft app registration, then waits for Run example query before querying.

Install fabricQueryR, odbc, bslib, processx, askpass and Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 first. You need an existing Fabric item and permission to use its data. See Getting started for editing and ?oauth_db_cloud_demo for the launcher settings.

Set up SQL access

In R, run install.packages(c("fabricQueryR", "odbc")). Install Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 for your operating system too. Copy the server and database from the item’s SQL connection settings. Users need access to that item and its data; see Fabric SQL connectivity.

Create an Entra Web app registration with permission to access SQL on a user’s behalf. Register http://localhost:8100 as its redirect URI. Save these values in a local .Renviron file and restart R:

OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID=your-tenant-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret

Use the Microsoft registration steps. For this first SQL app, add Azure SQL Database delegated user_impersonation. Fabric API permissions are needed only when adding the API examples later in this guide.

Value Where to find it
server Open the Warehouse or Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint, then copy its SQL connection string server
database The database/catalog shown in those connection settings
Tenant ID, client ID, secret Your Entra app registration

Copy the server hostname, without a connection-string prefix or credentials. Share the item with the app’s users and grant access to its data. A workspace or item ID from the browser URL isn’t the SQL server hostname.

A complete app

Save this as example.R, replacing the server and database:

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

client <- oauth_db_microsoft_client(
  services = "sql",
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_fabric_sql(
    auth$connection,
    server = "example.datawarehouse.fabric.microsoft.com",
    database = "Reporting"
  )

  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT CURRENT_USER AS database_user")
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

Run source("example.R") and open http://localhost:8100. Sign in to run the query; signing out clears the output.

The query shows the database user. Replace it with SQL for your tables. Call con() inside the reactive expression to get the DBI connection; you can also use it with dbplyr.

List workspaces

To list the workspaces a user can access, change the client’s services to services = c("sql", "fabric"). The Fabric preset requests and requires the delegated Workspace.Read.All and Item.Read.All permissions. Add both to the Entra registration alongside SQL access, even if this example only lists workspaces.

Add verbatimTextOutput("workspaces") to the UI and put this inside server():

fabric <- oauth_db_fabric_api(auth$connection)

output$workspaces <- renderPrint({
  fabric$call(fabricQueryR::fabric_workspaces)
})

Pass a fabricQueryR function and its arguments to $call(). The client supplies the user’s credentials and returns the function’s result.

Choose additional services

Include the services your app uses in oauth_db_microsoft_client() and configure their delegated permissions in the Entra registration:

services entry Use it for
"sql" Warehouse, Lakehouse SQL endpoint, and SQL Database
"fabric" Workspace and item discovery
"onelake" OneLake files and tables
"dax" Semantic model queries
"kql" KQL queries
"graphql" GraphQL queries

Users need access to each workspace and item they query. SQL, OneLake, and semantic models have their own permissions.

For KQL, include "kql" in the client’s services. With fabric created as above, replace the table output with:

output$rows <- renderTable({
  fabric$call(
    fabricQueryR::fabric_kql_query,
    cluster = "https://example.kusto.fabric.microsoft.com",
    database = "Events",
    query = "Events | take 20"
  )
})

Read a Lakehouse table

Use services = c("fabric", "onelake") to discover a Lakehouse and read its tables. Add these services to the client if you’re also using SQL.

fabric_item() returns a fabricQueryR object with methods such as $read_table(). Put the lookup inside reactive() so it runs again if the signed-in account changes:

lakehouse <- reactive({
  fabric$call(
    fabricQueryR::fabric_item,
    workspace = "workspace-guid",
    item = "lakehouse-guid"
  )
})

output$rows <- renderTable({
  lakehouse()$read_table("Orders", limit = 100L)
})

Warehouse objects offer $sql_query(sql), and semantic model objects offer $dax_query(dax). Include "sql" or "dax" in the client’s services for those methods. See fabricQueryR’s help for their arguments.

Connection options

The SQL helper uses ODBC by default, including SQL Server translations for dbplyr. Set timeout and read_only on the helper if your app needs different connection settings. For ADBC and Arrow connections, see ?oauth_db_fabric_sql and fabricQueryR::fabric_sql_connect().

Call con() before each operation. ODBC keeps a valid database session open through token renewal; ADBC replaces it on the next access. Consume and close outstanding results before starting another operation. Your app must also close any connections it opens directly through fabricQueryR functions or resource methods.

Use an existing sign-in

If your shinyOAuth client uses different token target names, map the services to those targets:

fabric <- oauth_db_fabric_api(
  auth$connection,
  targets = c(fabric = "discovery", sql = "reporting", onelake = "files")
)

The mapping replaces the defaults. For one service without a named target, use targets = list(kql = NULL). DAX and GraphQL share the Power BI resource and must use the same target; different resources need different targets.

To call a fabricQueryR function directly, pass token = fabric$token_provider(). ?oauth_db_fabric shows the alternative for a single service.

See Getting started for target settings and saved query results.
